title: Your Identity With Your Speech
learningGoals: Separate an event from a verdict

deeperExplanation.question: Does loosening identity mean lowering my standards?
deeperExplanation.answer: You can keep a high standard for the work while allowing the person doing it to learn. Before a meeting, a standard might help you check your facts. During the meeting, protecting an image of always being impressive may consume attention you need for the discussion. Try putting the standard in the preparation and the purpose in the conversation. Afterwards, review a specific action rather than deciding whether you lived up to your whole identity.

sections.narration:
Welcome. In this session, we will explore your identity with your speech: the picture you carry of yourself as a speaker. Perhaps you see yourself as someone who struggles to speak. Or perhaps people see you as confident, and you feel pressure to maintain that impression. Either picture can become something you feel you have to protect.

First, we will notice a speaking label. Then we will separate a particular event from a verdict about you. Finally, we will try a more specific description and a short speaking experiment. We will use examples, a simple diagram and your own observations. You can pause, ask me a question, or switch to reading at any point. You do not need to decide who you are before we begin.

sections.narration:
Here, identity means the descriptions you treat as statements about who you are. A description might be: I sometimes stammer. Another might be: I am a confident speaker. Descriptions can help us understand our experience. The question is how tightly we hold them.

A description can turn into a rule to protect. I must always sound confident gives you an extra job while you are trying to communicate. I am a poor speaker can make one difficult moment seem like proof of a permanent limit. These are different descriptions, but either can restrict what you feel free to try.

We are not asking you to remove your history, values or ambition. We are exploring whether one speaking moment needs to decide your whole identity.

visual.title: Description or rule?
labels: A rule to protect: I must always sound confident
visual.altText: A description names an experience. A rigid rule demands that you preserve an image.

sections.narration:
Imagine introducing yourself at a meeting. A speaking event happens: I repeated part of my name. An interpretation might be: They must think I am incapable. A wider conclusion might follow: I am a poor speaker. Notice that these are three different things. The event happened. The interpretation is a guess about other people. The conclusion stretches one moment into a statement about you.

A more specific account would be: I repeated part of my name during this introduction. That does not tell us everything about your ability, your value or how the meeting will go. You may still feel embarrassed. A specific description does not require pretending the moment felt good.

Now consider the opposite picture: I must always sound confident. One hesitation may feel threatening because it seems to contradict that image. You can value clear communication without requiring every attempt to protect an impressive identity. Keep the standard useful in preparation; give your message room during the conversation.

sections.narration: Think of a name badge that has become a suit of armour. It helped people recognise you, but now every movement has to fit inside it. You can put the badge on the table for one conversation. Your experience and values remain available. This is a way to picture a rigid description, not a claim that identity is something physical. You can keep the parts of a description that are useful and leave room for a new experience.

sections.narration:
Compare these statements. I am a poor speaker is a broad verdict. I repeated part of my name during this introduction describes a particular event. I must never hesitate in an important meeting is a performance rule.

A specific description gives you something you can explore: the situation, what you were trying to say, and how it felt. It does not demand a positive story. Now choose the statement that describes one speaking event.

sections.narration:
Think of a familiar description of yourself as a speaker. You can write it or say it privately. If it contains always, never or must, notice that word. You do not have to challenge every description or manufacture a positive replacement.

If useful, choose one recent situation and describe it more specifically: where you were, whom you were speaking with, and what happened. Keep what you know, and leave other people's unspoken opinions uncertain. Compare the two descriptions. Notice pressure, resistance, relief or no clear difference. You can also skip this reflection.

exercise.label: Guided rehearsal
exercise.scenario: You introduce yourself at a meeting. One word catches. Before the introduction is over, a verdict appears: I am not the confident person they thought I was. A short speaking event has become a conclusion about who you are.
partnerPrompts: Tell me something you enjoy outside work.

sections.narration:
What did you notice? Something may have changed, things may have felt much the same, or you may be unsure. Each is a valid observation. I cannot know what you felt just from whether words came easily.

Loosening identity does not mean pretending you have no history or that a difficult moment did not matter. It means allowing a description to stay open enough for another experience. If a label returns, you can notice it and return to the message. You do not need to argue with it until it disappears.

Does this mean lowering your standards? You can prepare carefully and still allow yourself to learn. After a conversation, review a specific action rather than deciding whether you lived up to your whole identity.

sections.narration:
There are two different places to use what we have explored. In focused practice, you can deliberately notice a label and try a specific observation. In a real conversation, give most of your attention to the message and the other person. You do not need to keep examining your identity while you speak.

A familiar support can be available if it helps. Choose one ordinary introduction this week and a small communication purpose, such as sharing one useful thing. Afterwards, if you want, describe one event without turning it into a verdict about yourself. You can leave the result uncertain.

sections.narration:
Three things to take with you. A speaking description is not the whole of who you are. One event can be described without becoming a permanent verdict. And a high standard can guide your preparation without becoming an image you must defend in every sentence.

Save one observation in your own words if you wish. You can finish here, practise this tool with a new prompt, or have a conversation where the focus is what you want to say. You choose the next step.
